speaker: Feng Zhang
title: 323 - CRISPR and the future of gene editing with Feng Zhang
question: In clinical gene editing for sickle cell disease, why do approved therapies modify a completely different gene instead of directly fixing the single-letter sickle mutation?
guest: The way the treatment works is that for sickle cell patients, it's been found that for some individuals who have the sickle cell mutation, if they also carry another mutation or if they somehow are able to express the fetal version of hemoglobin, then their sickle cell symptoms are much less. And so for treating sickle cell patients with gene editing, the therapy actually goes and modifies a different gene, modulating its expression to then allow the fetal hemoglobin gene to turn on. Because the way it works is that it simply makes a cut, and it doesn't require the template to repair.

points.core: Reactivating fetal hemoglobin expression substantially reduces clinical symptoms in sickle cell patients.
points.note: Accept: turning on HbF or fetal hemoglobin compensates for sickling or alleviates symptoms, mimicking protective natural mutations. Do not credit: vague statements about targeting a backup pathway without naming fetal hemoglobin.

points.core: The therapy disrupts a separate regulatory gene to switch fetal hemoglobin on.
points.note: Accept: modifying or knocking out a different repressor gene (such as BCL11A) to derepress or reactivate fetal hemoglobin. Do not credit: generic claims about indirect editing without explaining switching on another gene.

points.core: Disrupting a gene only requires a simple cut without template-directed DNA repair.
points.note: Accept: NHEJ or simple double-strand cleavage is far easier or more efficient than homology-directed repair (HDR) with a donor template to rewrite a base. Do not credit: generic claims that fixing the mutation is harder without citing the no-template cut mechanism.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer: Approved therapies like Casgevy don't directly correct the sickle mutation because disrupting a gene is far simpler and more reliable for current CRISPR tools than precisely rewriting a single DNA letter. Fixing the mutation would require homology-directed repair, which is inefficient in blood stem cells and risks unintended edits. Instead, Casgevy targets BCL11A, a gene whose protein normally switches off production of fetal hemoglobin after birth. By knocking out BCL11A specifically in red-blood-cell precursors, the therapy reactivates fetal hemoglobin, which doesn't carry the sickle defect and interferes with the sickling process. A simple disruptive cut at BCL11A is highly efficient, and patients who naturally retain fetal hemoglobin have milder disease, so there was strong evidence this approach works. This strategy also benefits beta-thalassemia, since boosting fetal hemoglobin compensates for deficient adult hemoglobin regardless of the specific mutation. So rather than repairing one defect letter-by-letter, the therapy reawakens a healthy backup hemoglobin the body already knows how to make.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Approved CRISPR gene editing for sickle cell disease, Casgevy, targets the erythroid enhancer of *BCL11A* rather than the mutated beta-globin gene (*HBB*) because disrupting DNA is far more efficient and safer with standard Cas9 nucleases than rewriting a single letter. Cas9 cuts both DNA strands, triggering two competing cellular repair pathways: error-prone non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and precise homology-directed repair (HDR). Directly correcting the *HBB* mutation requires HDR with a donor template, a pathway largely inactive in quiescent, long-term hematopoietic stem cells. Cutting *HBB* in these cells predominantly produces NHEJ insertions and deletions that abolish beta-globin expression, effectively converting sickle alleles into beta-thalassemia alleles, while risking off-target cuts and rearrangements at closely related globin genes. Conversely, NHEJ excels in stem cells when the goal is simply disabling a sequence. Disrupting the *BCL11A* enhancer silences the transcriptional repressor that normally shuts off fetal hemoglobin after birth, reactivating functional fetal hemoglobin that blocks sickling and allowing the same therapy to treat beta-thalassemia.

noweb.answer: Approved CRISPR therapy (Casgevy) targets *BCL11A* rather than directly correcting the *HBB* sickle mutation because disrupting DNA is far more efficient and safer in blood stem cells than precisely rewriting it. Standard Cas9 cuts both DNA strands, forcing the cell to repair the break. Fixing the single-letter *HBB* mutation requires homology-directed repair using an added DNA template, a pathway that works poorly in mostly non-dividing hematopoietic stem cells and impairs their engraftment. Instead, these cells predominantly rely on non-homologous end joining, an error-prone mechanism that introduces small insertions or deletions. Cutting *HBB* directly therefore risks scrambling the gene and causing beta-thalassemia more often than fixing it. By instead cutting an erythroid-specific enhancer of *BCL11A*, the repressor that silences fetal hemoglobin after birth, clinicians turn error-prone repair into an advantage. Those small edits reliably disable the switch in red blood cell precursors, reactivating healthy, anti-sickling fetal hemoglobin without a donor template. Newer base and prime editors rewrite *HBB* without double-strand breaks, but remain in clinical trials.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Directly correcting the single-letter sickle mutation in the beta-globin gene (*HBB*) with standard CRISPR-Cas9 is technically difficult in blood stem cells. Precisely rewriting DNA requires homology-directed repair (HDR) alongside a repair template, a pathway that operates inefficiently in largely non-dividing hematopoietic stem cells. Instead, those cells predominantly use non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), a faster but error-prone pathway that stitches broken DNA back together with small insertions or deletions. Cutting directly inside *HBB* risks creating disruptive edits that shut down beta-globin production altogether, potentially converting sickle cell disease into beta-thalassemia.

Approved CRISPR therapy (exagamglogene autotemcel, or Casgevy) turns NHEJ's strength into an advantage by disrupting the erythroid-specific enhancer of *BCL11A*, a gene that normally silences fetal hemoglobin after birth. Simply breaking this genetic switch requires no DNA template, works at high efficiency in stem cells, and reactivates fetal hemoglobin, which prevents red blood cells from sickling. As an added benefit, the same mutation-agnostic edit also treats transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia.

noweb.answer:
Approved CRISPR gene-editing therapy for sickle cell disease, such as exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy), targets an enhancer of the *BCL11A* gene rather than directly fixing the single-letter *HBB* mutation because of how human blood stem cells repair cut DNA. When standard Cas9 makes a double-strand break, cells overwhelmingly use an error-prone pathway called non-homologous end joining, which reliably disrupts a target sequence. Directly rewriting the sickle mutation instead requires homology-directed repair with a corrective DNA template—a process that is inefficient in resting hematopoietic stem cells and often leaves unintended insertions or deletions in *HBB*, potentially turning a sickle allele into a nonfunctional beta-thalassemia allele.

By contrast, disrupting the erythroid-specific switch on *BCL11A* plays to CRISPR's natural strength. Turning off *BCL11A* in red blood cell precursors reactivates fetal hemoglobin, which does not sickle and physically inhibits sickling of the mutant adult hemoglobin. This indirect strategy achieves far higher, safer editing efficiency in stem cells and works across both sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Casgevy edits a regulatory switch in **BCL11A** that normally shuts down fetal hemoglobin production in red blood cells after birth. Disabling that switch lets the cells make fetal hemoglobin again. Fetal hemoglobin interferes with the formation of the rigid fibers of sickle hemoglobin that deform red blood cells.

The choice is practical. Disabling the switch relies on a common DNA repair process that can efficiently disrupt it in blood-forming stem cells. Directly correcting the sickle mutation in **HBB** requires a precise single-letter change, which has been harder to achieve efficiently in the long-lived stem cells needed for a lasting treatment. Direct correction is still being studied.

Casgevy is the approved gene-editing therapy. Lyfgenia, another approved gene therapy, uses a different approach: it adds a modified beta-globin gene.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
The approved gene-editing therapy Casgevy targets a switch in a different gene because turning fetal hemoglobin back on can prevent sickling. After infancy, a protein called BCL11A normally turns down fetal hemoglobin production. Casgevy disrupts a DNA switch that controls BCL11A in developing red blood cells. Those cells then produce enough fetal hemoglobin to keep sickle hemoglobin from clumping into the fibers that distort their shape.

The choice also reflects what CRISPR can reliably do in long-lived blood stem cells. Disrupting a switch only requires the cell to repair a cut in a way that breaks the switch. Fixing the sickle mutation requires one exact DNA change. Direct correction is being studied, but disrupting the switch provided a practical, clinically proven way to protect red blood cells while leaving the sickle mutation in place.

The other approved genetic therapy, Lyfgenia, works differently. It adds a gene encoding an anti-sickling form of hemoglobin.
